Nagara（納加拉鼓）為膜鳴樂器，分布於印度、中亞與中東。印度常見成對使用，一: The nagara is a membranophone found in India, Central Asia and the Middle East. In India it is commonly played in pairs, one high and one low, struck with sticks, and used in temple ritual and at weddings; south Indian temples also use paired skin drums as festival instruments, with a hemispherical metal vessel below the body and the head held by rope or metal strips, struck with a special beater or a curved stick. In Central Asia and the Middle East it is mostly a single drum, in various sizes and under various names. In the Sikh tradition it is a large single drum, used in gatka displays and historically on the battlefield.

坐或站，將鼓置於身前合適位置。將鼓穩定放置於地面或夾於雙腿之間。用手掌或鼓棒敲擊: Sit or stand and set the drum in a comfortable position in front of you. Rest the drum steadily on the floor or hold it between the legs. Strike the centre or the edge of the head with the palm or a stick; different positions give different timbres. The force of the stroke sets the volume. It sounds by being struck, so watch the striking position and the control of force.

納加拉鼓具有明亮、清脆而富有穿透力的音色特徵。其高頻泛音豐富，敲擊時能發出鏗鏘有: The nagara has a bright, clear, penetrating timbre. Its high overtones are rich, and struck it gives a ringing, forceful sound; it lies high in pitch and has a strong sense of definite pitch. The way the head is tensioned makes the resonance quick and concentrated, and the vibration dies away fast; the timbre sits between metal and membrane, neither too heavy nor too thin. Compared with the deep, full bass drum it is more agile and alert; compared with the snare drum it is louder, with more complex overtones. In an ensemble it often plays both the backbone of the rhythm and a colour accent, and its sound carries and is easily picked out in a band.
納加拉鼓在印度教寺廟儀式與婚禮中出現，常以成對高音鼓與低音鼓搭配鼓棒演奏。南印度: The nagara appears in Hindu temple ritual and at weddings, usually in pairs of a high and a low drum played with sticks. In Tamil Nadu, south Indian temple instruments are used for daily worship, consecration, temple fairs, festivals, and processions of vehicles, floats and palanquins; famous temples tie pairs of drums to the backs of oxen or elephants and beat them before a procession, telling worshippers that the party is approaching. The Sikh tradition uses a large single drum for gatka (Gatka) martial-arts displays, and historically on the battlefield. In Central Asia and the Middle East it is mostly a single drum, with names for large, small, stick, armpit and hand types according to size and how it is held.
納加拉鼓為膜鳴樂器，來源記載其鼓身下半部為半球形金屬容器，金屬部分可能為黃銅或銅: The nagara is a membranophone; the source records that the lower half of the body is a hemispherical metal vessel, possibly of brass or copper, and that the head is of goatskin or a similar membrane, fixed to the vessel with rope or metal strips. It is struck with a special beater or a curved stick. The source does not state the materials of other regions or forms.
納加拉鼓起源於中東和南亞地區，是一種古老的雙面鼓樂器。其名稱源自阿拉伯語「Naq: The nagara originated in the Middle East and South Asia and is an ancient double-headed drum. Its name comes from the Arabic 'Naqqāra', meaning a drum beaten with a stick. The drum was widely used in the medieval Islamic empire, above all in the Ottoman military bands, where it became an important military instrument.
納加拉鼓隨著伊斯蘭文明的擴張，逐漸傳入印度、波斯和土耳其等地區，並在各地發展出不: As Islamic civilisation expanded, the nagara spread to India, Persia and Turkey, and each region developed its own forms and playing styles. In the Indian classical tradition it was taken into chamber music and religious music. The instrument usually consists of a hemispherical resonator of copper or wood with an animal-skin head, often played in pairs, and different striking techniques produce a variety of timbres. The nagara keeps an important place in traditional musical culture and is still widely used in the folk music of the Middle East, South Asia and North Africa.
